The robustness check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification. Disaggregation systematically deteriorates out-of-sample \(R^2\) across all four ML models and both coffee varieties, with every \(ΔR^2\) value negative. The deterioration is moderate for Random Forest (\(ΔR^2\) of −0.044 for Arabica, −0.115 for Robusta) and XGBoost (−0.020 and −0.058), but severe for SVM and ANN, which produce negative \(R^2\) values under the disaggregated specification, indicating performance worse than a naive mean forecast.

This pattern is consistent with the curse of dimensionality: with 40 regressors and approximately 170 training observations, models sensitive to input dimensionality become severely overparameterised and fail to generalise to the test period. The ensemble methods Random Forest and XGBoost are more robust to this problem through their built-in variable selection mechanisms, but still suffer a meaningful performance loss. These results suggest that the production-weighted aggregation improves the climate signal by filtering out country-specific noise, and that the information gain from disaggregation is outweighed by the dimensionality cost at the sample sizes available in this study.

4.9 Variety-Specific Model Specification

The robustness check conducted in the preceding section validated the production-weighted aggregation methodology by showing that disaggregated climate indices systematically deteriorate out-of-sample performance. A second robustness check is now conducted by re-estimating all six models under a variety-specific specification. Rather than using global climate indices and world supply-and-demand fundamentals, this specification assigns each model its own set of variety-relevant predictors: the Arabica models use climate indices and fundamentals aggregated across the ten Arabica-producing countries, while the Robusta models use the equivalent aggregates for the six Robusta-producing countries. This specification is motivated by the structural concentration of Robusta production in Vietnam and Indonesia (approximately 67% combined) and the broader geographic diversification of Arabica production. Using global indices for Robusta in particular dilutes the climate and supply signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually no Robusta.

This chunk defines the variety-specific exogenous variable lists and prepares the two datasets used in the re-estimation below. Sample sizes are printed to the console for verification.

Sample sizes for the variety-specific datasets mirror those of the baseline specification, 168 training and 43 test observations for Arabica, and 153 training and 39 test observations for Robusta, confirming that the variety-specific variable substitution does not alter the temporal coverage of either dataset.

All six models are re-estimated under this specification using the same walk-forward protocol as the baseline. The Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM and ANN models reuse the generic functions already defined in the disaggregated robustness check above, called here with the variety-specific variable lists. ARIMAX and MLR are generalised below by adding a vars_exo_vec argument following the same pattern.

The chunk below defines the generic ARIMAX and MLR functions and re-estimates all six models under the variety-specific specification.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — GENERIC ARIMAX FUNCTION
# Identical to fit_arimax() defined earlier, except that the
# predictor list is passed in as vars_exo_vec rather than
# always using the global vars_exo. This allows the function
# to be called with any predictor list without modification.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_arimax_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  serie_dependante    <- df[[var_dep]]
  matrice_regresseurs <- as.matrix(df[, vars_exo_vec])

  colonnes_valides    <- apply(matrice_regresseurs, 2,
                               function(col) !all(is.na(col)))
  matrice_regresseurs <- matrice_regresseurs[, colonnes_valides, drop = FALSE]

  n_total    <- length(serie_dependante)
  y_train    <- serie_dependante[1:n_train]
  y_test     <- serie_dependante[(n_train + 1):n_total]
  xreg_train <- matrice_regresseurs[1:n_train, ]
  xreg_test  <- matrice_regresseurs[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test     <- length(y_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_observations_vues <- i - 1
    indices_vus          <- seq_len(nb_observations_vues)
    y_vu                 <- y_test[indices_vus]
    xreg_vu              <- xreg_test[indices_vus, , drop = FALSE]
    y_fenetre            <- c(y_train, y_vu)
    xreg_fenetre         <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_vu)

    modele_arima <- tryCatch(
      auto.arima(y_fenetre, xreg = xreg_fenetre,
                 stepwise = TRUE, approximation = TRUE,
                 max.p = 3, max.q = 3, max.d = 1),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_arima)) { predictions[i] <- NA; next }

    ligne_regresseurs_futurs <- matrix(xreg_test[i, ], nrow = 1)
    prevision <- forecast(modele_arima, h = 1,
                          xreg = ligne_regresseurs_futurs)
    predictions[i] <- prevision$mean[1]
  }

  list(actual = y_test, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — GENERIC MLR FUNCTION
# Identical to fit_mlr() defined earlier, except that the
# predictor list is passed in as vars_exo_vec. intersect()
# ensures only columns present in df are used, guarding
# against any name mismatch between the variable list and
# the dataset columns.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_mlr_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele)
  donnees_train <- df_modele[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_ols           <- lm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement)
    predictions[i]       <- predict(modele_ols, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — RUN ALL SIX MODELS ON BOTH SERIES
# Each model is called twice: once for Arabica using
# df_arabica_vs and vars_exo_ara_vs, and once for Robusta
# using df_robusta_vs and vars_exo_rob_vs. The four ML
# generic functions were defined in the disaggregated
# robustness check chunk and are reused here unchanged.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running variety-specific ARIMAX - Arabica...\n")
res_arimax_ara_vs <- fit_arimax_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                          vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific ARIMAX - Robusta...\n")
res_arimax_rob_vs <- fit_arimax_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                          vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific MLR - Arabica...\n")
res_mlr_ara_vs <- fit_mlr_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific MLR - Robusta...\n")
res_mlr_rob_vs <- fit_mlr_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific RF - Arabica...\n")
res_rf_ara_vs <- fit_rf_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                  vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific RF - Robusta...\n")
res_rf_rob_vs <- fit_rf_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                  vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific XGBoost - Arabica...\n")
res_xgb_ara_vs <- fit_xgb_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific XGBoost - Robusta...\n")
res_xgb_rob_vs <- fit_xgb_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific SVM - Arabica...\n")
res_svm_ara_vs <- fit_svm_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific SVM - Robusta...\n")
res_svm_rob_vs <- fit_svm_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific ANN - Arabica...\n")
res_ann_ara_vs <- fit_ann_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific ANN - Robusta...\n")
res_ann_rob_vs <- fit_ann_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — STACK PERFORMANCE METRICS
# calculer_metriques() is applied to each model's actual and
# predicted vectors. Results are stacked into a single 12-row
# data frame (6 models × 2 series) and numeric columns are
# coerced from character to numeric as in metriques_all.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_vs_all <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_ara_vs$actual, res_arimax_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_rob_vs$actual, res_arimax_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_ara_vs$actual, res_mlr_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_rob_vs$actual, res_mlr_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_ara_vs$actual, res_rf_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_rob_vs$actual, res_rf_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_ara_vs$actual, res_xgb_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_rob_vs$actual, res_xgb_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_ara_vs$actual, res_svm_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_rob_vs$actual, res_svm_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara_vs$actual, res_ann_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob_vs$actual, res_ann_rob_vs$predicted))
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric))

The table and chart below compare the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of each model under the baseline and variety-specific specifications. A positive \(ΔR^2\) indicates improvement under the variety-specific specification; a negative value indicates deterioration.

Show code 
library(ggh4x)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — BUILD THE COMPARISON DATA FRAME
# The baseline R² from metriques_all is joined to the
# variety-specific R² from metriques_vs_all. Delta_R2 is
# the difference between the two, positive values indicating
# improvement under the variety-specific specification.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_comparison_vs <- metriques_all %>%
  select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
  mutate(R2 = as.numeric(R2)) %>%
  rename(R2_baseline = R2) %>%
  left_join(
    metriques_vs_all %>%
      select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
      rename(R2_vs = R2),
    by = c("Model", "Series")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_R2    = round(R2_vs - R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_baseline = round(R2_baseline, 4),

df_comparison_vs %>%

  kable(caption   = "Baseline vs variety-specific specification — out-of-sample R²",

  pack_rows("Robusta", 7, 12,
            bold       = TRUE,

            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(
    df_comparison_vs %>%
      arrange(Series, desc(R2_baseline)) %>%
      pull(Delta_R2) > 0,
    "darkgreen", "red"))

The variety-specific specification yields asymmetric results across the two coffee varieties, revealing an important structural difference in how variety-relevant climate and supply information contributes to predictive accuracy.

For Robusta, the variety-specific specification improves out-of-sample performance for four of the six models. ARIMAX gains marginally (+0.008, \(R^2\) = 0.937), while Random Forest (+0.029) and XGBoost (+0.053) show more meaningful improvements, with XGBoost in particular reaching \(R^2\) = 0.849 under the variety-specific specification, its strongest result across all configurations tested in this study. This confirms the central hypothesis motivating this robustness check: using climate indices and fundamentals restricted to the six Robusta-producing countries provides more relevant supply-side information than the global aggregates, which dilute the Robusta signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually none. The improvement is most pronounced for the gradient boosting models, which are best placed to exploit the more targeted non-linear relationships between Robusta-specific supply conditions and price dynamics.

For Arabica, the picture is reversed. All six models deteriorate under the variety-specific specification, with ARIMAX losing 0.177 \(R^2\) points and ANN producing a negative \(R^2\) of −0.413. The reasons for this deterioration are discussed in the limitations section.

Taken together, these results suggest that variety-specific predictors are a genuine improvement for Robusta but not for Arabica, where the global specification already captures the relevant producing-country conditions. The XGBoost model under the Robusta variety-specific specification (\(R^2\)= 0.849) represents the strongest result for that variety across all configurations and specifications estimated in this study.

4.10 Robustness Check: OECD GDP Growth (Quarterly Specification)

This robustness check addresses a variable suggested during supervision: OECD real GDP growth, a demand-side macroeconomic indicator published only at quarterly frequency, with no monthly equivalent available. Incorporating it therefore requires moving estimation to quarterly frequency rather than approximating it within the monthly pipeline. Because changing frequency and adding a predictor are two distinct changes, three configurations are compared rather than two: the monthly baseline already reported in the comparative performance section, a quarterly configuration that aggregates the same 14 baseline predictors without GDP growth, and a quarterly configuration that adds GDP growth as a fifteenth predictor. Comparing the second and third configurations isolates the marginal contribution of GDP growth at a fixed quarterly frequency. All six models are re-estimated using the generic functions already defined for the preceding robustness checks.

The chunk below reads the OECD quarterly GDP series, aggregates the monthly dataset to quarterly frequency, and builds the two quarterly dataset variants used in the re-estimation below.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — READ THE OECD QUARTERLY GDP SERIES
# Quarter labels are in row 5, growth rates in row 8, both
# starting at column 3 of the raw OECD export file. The
# "trimestre" label is renamed to "date" so that the existing
# preparer_niveaux_vs() function can be reused unchanged in
# the next chunk — it only requires a column called "date"
# to sort on, regardless of its granularity.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_pib_raw <- read_excel(FICHIER_PIB, col_names = FALSE)

trimestres <- as.character(df_pib_raw[5, 3:ncol(df_pib_raw)])
pib_vals   <- as.numeric(df_pib_raw[8, 3:ncol(df_pib_raw)])

df_pib <- data.frame(date       = trimestres,
                     pib_growth = pib_vals,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(pib_growth), grepl("Q", date)) %>%
  filter(date >= "2000-Q1" & date <= "2023-Q4") %>%
  arrange(date)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — AGGREGATE THE MONTHLY DATASET TO QUARTERLY
# Every numeric column of dataset_mensuel is averaged within
# each quarter. na.rm = TRUE means a quarter with only one or
# two valid months (e.g. June 2006 for cot_net_mm, the first
# month the COT report exists) still produces a non-missing
# average from the months available. Quarters with zero valid
# months (e.g. cot_net_mm before mid-2006, robusta_price
# before 2008) correctly produce NaN, which is.na() treats
# as missing.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dataset_trimestriel_base <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  mutate(date = paste0(
    substr(date, 1, 4), "-Q",
    ceiling(as.integer(substr(date, 6, 7)) / 3)
  )) %>%
  select(-date_fmt) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(date >= "2000-Q1" & date <= "2023-Q4") %>%
  arrange(date)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — BUILD THE TWO QUARTERLY DATASET VARIANTS
# dataset_trimestriel_nogdp: the 14 baseline predictors at
# quarterly frequency, no GDP — isolates the frequency effect.
# dataset_trimestriel_gdp: the same base, plus GDP growth —
# the variant of primary interest in this robustness check.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dataset_trimestriel_nogdp <- dataset_trimestriel_base

dataset_trimestriel_gdp <- dataset_trimestriel_base %>%
  left_join(df_pib, by = "date")

cat("Quarterly base - rows:", nrow(dataset_trimestriel_base), "\n")
cat("Quarters with available GDP growth:",
    sum(!is.na(dataset_trimestriel_gdp$pib_growth)), "\n")

The quarterly base dataset contains 96 rows, matching the expected 288 months divided into 96 quarters with full coverage from 2000-Q1 to 2023-Q4. All 96 quarters have an available GDP growth observation, confirming that the OECD series introduces no additional missing-data constraint beyond those already present in the baseline predictors.

The chunk below defines the variable lists for the two quarterly variants, prepares the four datasets (two series × two specifications), and computes the 80/20 train/test split indices used in the re-estimation below.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — VARIABLE LISTS FOR THE TWO VARIANTS
# The "no GDP" variant reuses the global vars_exo list (14
# predictors) already defined in the preprocessing chunk.
# The "with GDP" variant adds pib_growth as a 15th predictor.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo_pib <- c(vars_exo, "pib_growth")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 — PREPARE THE FOUR QUARTERLY DATASETS
# preparer_niveaux_vs() is reused unchanged from the
# variety-specific robustness check — it only requires a
# "date" column to sort on and a vars_exo_vec argument,
# both satisfied here.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_arabica_trim_nogdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_nogdp, "arabica_price", vars_exo)

df_robusta_trim_nogdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_nogdp %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)),
  "robusta_price", vars_exo)

df_arabica_trim_gdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_gdp, "arabica_price", vars_exo_pib)

df_robusta_trim_gdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_gdp %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)),
  "robusta_price", vars_exo_pib)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 6 — 80/20 SPLIT, SAME split_ratio AS EVERY OTHER MODEL
# ----------------------------------------------------------

n_train_ara_trim_nogdp <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_trim_nogdp) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_trim_nogdp <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_trim_nogdp) * split_ratio)
n_train_ara_trim_gdp   <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_trim_gdp)   * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_trim_gdp   <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_trim_gdp)   * split_ratio)

cat("Arabica quarterly, no GDP   - Train:", n_train_ara_trim_nogdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_trim_nogdp) - n_train_ara_trim_nogdp, "\n")
cat("Robusta quarterly, no GDP   - Train:", n_train_rob_trim_nogdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_trim_nogdp) - n_train_rob_trim_nogdp, "\n")
cat("Arabica quarterly, with GDP - Train:", n_train_ara_trim_gdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_trim_gdp) - n_train_ara_trim_gdp, "\n")
cat("Robusta quarterly, with GDP - Train:", n_train_rob_trim_gdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_trim_gdp) - n_train_rob_trim_gdp, "\n")

The resulting training and test sizes are 56 and 15 quarters for Arabica and 51 and 13 quarters for Robusta, identical across the two variants since GDP growth does not remove any additional observation. The Arabica sample is constrained by the COT report, available only from June 2006, while the Robusta sample is constrained by its own data availability from 2008 onward, the same binding constraints as in the monthly specification, simply expressed in quarters rather than months. All six models are re-estimated using the generic functions already defined in the preceding robustness checks (fit_arimax_generique, fit_mlr_generique, fit_rf_generique, fit_xgb_generique, fit_svm_generique, fit_ann_generique), called here with the quarterly datasets and either the baseline vars_exo list or the extended vars_exo_pib list.

  df_robusta_trim_gdp, "robusta_price", vars_exo_pib, n_train_rob_trim_gdp)

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Baseline R² is pulled directly from metriques_all, never

df_robustness_pib <- metriques_all %>%
  select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
  mutate(R2 = as.numeric(R2)) %>%
  rename(R2_mensuel = R2) %>%

    by = c("Model", "Series")

  left_join(

      select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
      rename(R2_trim_gdp = R2),
    by = c("Model", "Series")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_GDP     = round(R2_trim_gdp - R2_trim_nogdp, 4),
    R2_mensuel    = round(R2_mensuel, 4),
    R2_trim_nogdp = round(R2_trim_nogdp, 4),
    R2_trim_gdp   = round(R2_trim_gdp, 4)
  )

The comparison across the three configurations isolates two distinct effects: moving from monthly to quarterly frequency, and adding GDP growth as a predictor once frequency is held fixed. The frequency effect dominates. For Arabica, the two econometric benchmarks tolerate the change reasonably well, with ARIMAX falling only marginally from 0.821 to 0.815 and MLR even improving slightly to 0.820, while the four machine learning models deteriorate substantially, most severely ANN, which collapses from 0.453 to −0.951. For Robusta, the deterioration is broader and affects every model: ARIMAX, the strongest performer in the monthly baseline at 0.929, drops to 0.552 at quarterly frequency, and MLR turns negative at −0.054. The most plausible explanation is sample size. The quarterly training window covers only 56 observations for Arabica and 51 for Robusta, against 168 and 153 at monthly frequency, a reduction that disproportionately penalises the more data-hungry machine learning models, in particular ANN and SVM.

Once frequency is held fixed, the addition of GDP growth produces no consistent improvement. For Arabica, five of the six models deteriorate further, in two cases substantially: SVM loses 0.123 of \(R^2\) and ANN, already negative, falls another 0.800 to −1.751. For Robusta, the picture is mixed but the gains are small relative to the losses. ARIMAX, MLR and XGBoost improve marginally, by between 0.002 and 0.009 points, Random Forest deteriorates marginally, and SVM loses more than a fifth of its \(R^2\) at −0.224. The one substantial gain, ANN at +0.201, starts from a negative baseline and still leaves the model only modestly above zero.

Taken together, these results provide no support for including GDP growth as a predictor. Its marginal contribution is small, inconsistently signed across models and series, and dwarfed by the cost of moving to quarterly frequency in the first place.

5 Discussion

5.1 Interpretation of Results

5.1.1 Overall Model Performance

The out-of-sample results present a consistent and interpretable picture of predictive performance across the six model families. Two broad conclusions emerge. First, models that explicitly account for the temporal dynamics of price series, whether through autoregressive components as in ARIMAX or through gradient boosting on trending levels as in XGBoost, systematically outperform static linear specifications. Second, the performance gap between the strongest and weakest models is substantially wider for Robusta than for Arabica, reflecting the more volatile and structurally demanding nature of the Robusta test period.

For Arabica, ARIMAX and XGBoost achieve near-identical \(R^2\) values of 0.821 and 0.818 respectively, confirming that the autoregressive structure of price dynamics carries predictive information that neither purely cross-sectional nor purely tree-based specifications can fully replicate. The forecast trajectory plots show that both models track the broad price level and direction correctly throughout the 2021–2024 test period, including the gradual rise through 2022 and the subsequent decline, though both exhibit the typical one-step-ahead lag at turning points. Random Forest follows closely at \(R^2\) = 0.811 and SVM at 0.813 following hyperparameter tuning, while MLR achieves \(R^2\) = 0.784, a result that reflects the strong trending co-movement between Arabica prices and the macroeconomic variables in levels rather than genuine structural predictive power. The ANN trails at 0.453 for reasons discussed in the limitations section.

For Robusta, the performance hierarchy shifts markedly. ARIMAX delivers the strongest result under the baseline specification with \(R^2\) = 0.929, driven by the strongly persistent autoregressive structure of Robusta prices over the test period, which was characterised by a near-monotonic upward trend that a high-persistence AR model naturally tracks well. XGBoost follows at \(R^2\) = 0.796, while SVM and Random Forest achieve 0.723 and 0.695 respectively. The most striking result is the collapse of MLR to \(R^2\) = 0.276, with forecast trajectories that oscillate erratically around the observed series and produce large directional errors. This failure reflects the well-known sensitivity of OLS to multicollinearity in short samples: with only 153 training observations and 14 highly collinear predictors, as documented in the correlation and PCA analyses, coefficient estimates become unstable and the model cannot generalise to the test period. This result underscores the importance of temporal dynamics in commodity price modelling and confirms that a static linear specification is insufficient for Robusta price prediction over the available sample.

The coefficient tables from the ARIMAX training-set estimation further illuminate the challenge of identifying interpretable linear relationships in this predictor space. For both varieties, only a small number of regressors reach conventional significance thresholds: Sugar and WTI for Arabica, CPI, WTI and COT net MM for Robusta. This outcome is not a failure of specification but a direct consequence of the severe multicollinearity documented in the correlation and PCA analyses, where Production, Consumption and Exports load almost identically on the first principal component. In the presence of such collinearity, OLS distributes explanatory power across correlated regressors in an unstable way, inflating standard errors and suppressing individual t-statistics even when the collective predictive content of the variable group is substantial. This observation provides a retrospective justification for the machine learning approach adopted in this study: Random Forest and XGBoost are specifically designed to exploit the predictive information contained in groups of correlated variables through non-linear combinations and variable selection mechanisms that are unavailable to the linear regression component of ARIMAX.

The overall level of predictive accuracy achieved, with \(R^2\) values generally above 0.75 across the best-performing models for both varieties, is worth noting in context. These results are obtained on series in levels, and the co-trending of prices with macroeconomic variables may inflate \(R^2\) beyond what would be achievable on stationary first-differenced series. This point is addressed explicitly in the limitations section.

5.1.2 The Role of Financial and Speculative Variables

The variable importance analysis from the Random Forest model provides the clearest picture of which predictors drive out-of-sample accuracy. For Arabica, Sugar No.11 prices and the COT net Managed Money position emerge as the two dominant predictors, contributing approximately 27% and 24% increase in MSE respectively when permuted, well above all other variables. The dominance of speculative positioning reflects the progressive financialisation of the Arabica market: the Coffee C contract on ICE Futures U.S. is among the most actively traded agricultural futures contracts, and the net position of Managed Money participants captures market-wide expectations about future price direction that are not yet reflected in contemporaneous fundamentals. The strong predictive power of COT net MM at the one-month-ahead horizon suggests that this sentiment signal is not fully incorporated into current prices, creating a forecasting opportunity that the Random Forest exploits through its non-linear variable interactions.

The prominence of Sugar No.11 prices in the Arabica ranking reflects the supply-side linkage between the two commodities in Brazil, the world’s largest producer of both. When sugar prices rise relative to coffee prices, the relative return to sugar cultivation increases, creating an incentive for land reallocation that is anticipated by market participants and reflected in coffee futures prices before it appears in realised production data. At monthly frequency, this anticipatory co-movement is directly exploitable by the model.

For Robusta, the importance hierarchy differs markedly in its upper ranks. WTI and CPI are the two dominant predictors, contributing approximately 25% and 22% increase in MSE respectively, displacing the financial and market-specific variables that led the Arabica ranking. The stronger role of energy costs for Robusta is consistent with the production geography of this variety: Vietnam and Indonesia, which together account for approximately 45% of world Robusta production, are major energy importers whose production and export logistics are more sensitive to global oil prices than the more diversified Brazilian Arabica supply chain. The prominence of CPI reflects the fact that Robusta is primarily consumed in price-sensitive market segments, including soluble coffee and value blends, where demand responds more elastically to the general price level than in the premium Arabica segment.

Across both varieties, financial and macroeconomic variables systematically outrank supply-side fundamentals and climate variables in terms of predictive contribution at monthly frequency. This finding carries a practical implication: short-run price signals for coffee are more reliably extracted from financial positioning data and macroeconomic indicators than from production and inventory statistics, which are published at annual frequency and carry substantial measurement uncertainty.

5.1.3 Climate Variables and the Lag Structure Problem

A consistent finding across both varieties is the relatively low variable importance of the climate indices compared to financial and macroeconomic predictors. For Arabica, Precipitation and Temperature rank last among all 14 predictors, each contributing approximately 3% and 6% increase in MSE respectively when permuted. For Robusta, the climate variables rank somewhat higher at approximately 6% and 8%, but remain well below the dominant financial and macro variables.

This result should not be interpreted as evidence that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices. Rather, it reflects a fundamental mismatch between the one-step-ahead monthly forecasting horizon of the models and the lag structure through which climate affects prices. Coffee cherry development, flowering and yield are influenced by temperature and precipitation conditions during the growing season, which typically spans six to twelve months before harvest. A climate shock in month \(t\) affects production in month \(t+6\) to \(t+12\), which in turn affects prices at a further lag as supply shortfalls propagate through inventories and trade flows. A contemporaneous monthly model cannot capture this transmission channel directly, and the climate signal is therefore largely absorbed by the production and ending stocks variables that already reflect the cumulative impact of past weather conditions on realised supply.

The ONI index, which captures ENSO conditions, ranks somewhat higher than the national climate indices for both varieties, contributing approximately 17% increase in MSE for Arabica and 16% for Robusta. This relatively stronger importance likely reflects the fact that ENSO episodes affect prices not only through realised supply but also through expectation formation: market participants anticipate the supply consequences of El Niño and La Niña episodes before they materialise in production data, creating a contemporaneous price effect that a monthly model can capture. This expectational channel is absent from the national temperature and precipitation indices, which measure realised meteorological conditions rather than forward-looking anomaly signals.

The implication for future model design is clear. Incorporating lagged climate variables at horizons of three, six and twelve months would allow the model to capture the delayed transmission from weather conditions to coffee prices through the production and inventory channel.

5.1.4 Arabica vs Robusta: Structural Differences

The contrast between Arabica and Robusta results across models reveals structural differences between the two markets that go beyond the shorter sample available for Robusta.

The dominance of ARIMAX on Robusta (\(R^2\) = 0.929 vs 0.821 for Arabica) reflects the stronger autoregressive persistence of Robusta prices over the test period. The ARIMA(3,0,1) error structure selected for Robusta, compared to ARIMA(1,0,0) for Arabica, indicates that Robusta price dynamics involve more complex short-run autocorrelation patterns, which ARIMAX captures through its MA component in addition to the AR terms. The near-monotonic upward trend in Robusta prices during the 2021–2024 test period further amplifies the advantage of an autoregressive model, which extrapolates a persistent trend more naturally than models that rely on cross-sectional variation among predictors.

The failure of MLR on Robusta but not Arabica is partly a sample size effect, with 153 versus 211 training observations, but also reflects the more pronounced multicollinearity among Robusta predictors. Robusta production is geographically concentrated in Vietnam and Indonesia, meaning that supply shocks are more correlated with specific macroeconomic conditions in those countries, which in turn co-move with global macro variables. This amplifies the collinearity problem relative to Arabica, where production is more geographically diversified across twelve countries spanning different climatic zones and economic environments.

The relatively weaker performance of tree-based models on Robusta, with Random Forest at \(R^2\) = 0.695 and XGBoost at 0.796 compared to their Arabica counterparts of 0.811 and 0.818, reflects the extrapolation limitation of ensemble methods. Random Forest and XGBoost average over training observations and cannot produce predictions that substantially exceed the range of target values seen during training. The sharp upward acceleration in Robusta prices from mid-2023 onward moves beyond the price range of the training set, causing both models to produce forecasts that flatten while the observed series continues rising. This limitation is clearly visible in the forecast trajectory and residual plots, where a persistent negative bias emerges for both tree-based models from late 2022 onward.

5.1.5 Robustness of the Methodology

The three robustness checks conducted in this study provide complementary evidence on the sensitivity of the main results to key methodological choices.

The disaggregated climate robustness check provides strong validation of the production-weighted aggregation approach. Replacing the two aggregated indices with the 28 individual national series systematically deteriorates out-of-sample \(R^2\) across all four ML models and both coffee varieties, with every \(ΔR^2\) value negative. The degradation is moderate for Random Forest and XGBoost but severe for SVM and ANN, which produce negative \(R^2\) values under the disaggregated specification. This pattern is consistent with the curse of dimensionality: with 40 regressors and approximately 170 training observations, models sensitive to input dimensionality become severely overparameterised. Beyond the dimensionality argument, the results suggest that production-weighted aggregation improves the climate signal by averaging out country-specific noise and idiosyncratic seasonal patterns that are irrelevant to global price formation. The aggregation methodology is therefore validated both statistically and economically.

The variety-specific robustness check yields asymmetric results that reveal an important structural difference between the two markets. For Robusta, restricting climate indices and fundamentals to the six actual Robusta-producing countries improves performance for four of the six models, with XGBoost reaching its strongest result across all configurations at \(R^2\) = 0.849. This improvement is economically intuitive: global indices dilute the Robusta climate and supply signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually no Robusta, and restricting to Vietnam, Indonesia, Uganda, Côte d’Ivoire, India and Brazil provides more targeted information about the supply conditions that actually drive Robusta prices. For Arabica, all six models deteriorate under the variety-specific specification. The global indices are in practice already dominated by Arabica-producing countries, as Brazil alone accounts for approximately 39% of world coffee production and approximately 47% of the Arabica-specific weight, so switching specifications changes the climate indices only marginally while simultaneously reducing the information content of the supply-demand fundamentals by excluding Robusta-producing countries whose consumption and export activity also influences global price formation.

The OECD GDP growth robustness check provides no support for including this variable as a predictor. Moving from monthly to quarterly frequency alone substantially degrades performance for most models, most severely for ANN, which collapses from \(R^2\) = 0.453 to $-$0.951 for Arabica. Once frequency is held fixed, the addition of GDP growth produces no consistent improvement across models or varieties. This negative result is consistent with the information already contained in the baseline predictor set: once CPI, the Federal Funds Rate, world consumption and the dollar index are included, OECD GDP growth carries little additional demand-side information at the frequency relevant for coffee futures pricing. The result also reflects a fundamental feasibility constraint: GDP growth has no monthly equivalent, so testing its contribution necessarily means testing it jointly with a frequency change that, on its own, already degrades out-of-sample performance. A genuinely monthly test of the variable’s marginal contribution is therefore not feasible with the data available.

5.2 Limitations

5.2.1 Non-Stationarity and Spurious Regression

The most significant methodological limitation of this study concerns the treatment of non-stationarity in the machine learning models. As established in the stationarity analysis, the majority of variables, including both dependent price series and most macroeconomic and fundamental predictors, are integrated of order one. The ARIMAX model handles this internally through the differencing parameter selected by auto.arima(), and the absence of differencing in the final specifications (\(d=0\)for both series) reflects the absorption of the common trend by the exogenous regressors. For the ML models, estimating on levels rather than first differences raises the spurious regression concern: two independently trending series will exhibit high \(R^2\) in levels even in the absence of any genuine predictive relationship.

The decision to estimate ML models on levels was motivated by the empirical finding that first-differenced specifications produced near-zero \(R^2\) values, confirming that month-to-month price changes are largely unpredictable at this frequency. While this decision is pragmatically defensible, as the models exploit genuine trending co-movement among fundamentally linked variables rather than spurious correlations between unrelated series, it implies that the reported \(R^2\) values for the ML models reflect in part the shared trend component of the series rather than purely their ability to forecast price dynamics. Future work could address this through cointegration-based specifications that model the long-run equilibrium relationship between prices and fundamentals while correcting for short-run deviations.

5.2.2 ANN Instability

The Artificial Neural Network implemented via the nnet package exhibits notable instability in the walk-forward forecasting setting. With only approximately 170 training observations at the early test steps and 75 connection weights to estimate for the 5-neuron Arabica architecture, the network is susceptible to converging to local minima that produce extreme predictions for isolated observations. A fixed random seed partially mitigates but does not eliminate this problem, as the loss landscape of a feedforward network contains multiple local optima of varying quality. The pronounced upward spikes visible in the ANN forecast trajectory plots for both varieties are a direct manifestation of this instability. More robust implementations would require ensemble averaging across multiple random initialisations, explicit regularisation such as L2 weight decay or dropout, or recurrent architectures such as Long Short-Term Memory networks that are specifically designed for sequential data and maintain a hidden state across time steps rather than reinitialising at each walk-forward step.

5.2.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity

The hyperparameter tuning procedure used for both SVM and ANN relies on a single chronological pre-loop split of the initial training window rather than a fully nested walk-forward search. This means that the selected hyperparameters minimise error on one specific validation window rather than across the full range of training window sizes encountered during the walk-forward loop. For ANN in particular, the tuning search selected a 3-neuron architecture for Robusta that performs worse out-of-sample than larger architectures would, illustrating the known sensitivity of small feedforward networks to the choice of validation window. Retaining the tuned architecture is the methodologically consistent choice, as selecting hyperparameters based on test set performance would violate the walk-forward validation protocol, but this result highlights the importance of more robust tuning procedures in future work.

5.2.4 Climate Data Resolution

The national climate averages used to construct the production-weighted indices are computed as simple arithmetic means across all ADM1 regions within each country, without intra-country production weights. This implies that non-producing regions contribute equally to the national average as major producing areas. For Brazil, for example, the Amazon basin carries the same weight as the coffee-producing states of Minas Gerais and São Paulo, attenuating the climate signal in countries with large non-producing territories. Sub-national production data at the ADM1 level are not systematically available from the USDA FAS PSD database, making intra-country production weighting infeasible with the data collected for this study. Future work could address this using remote sensing-based estimates of coffee cultivation area at high spatial resolution to construct more targeted intra-country weights.

5.2.5 Data Availability Constraints

Two structural data gaps restrict the estimation sample for certain model specifications. Robusta futures prices are available only from January 2008, reducing the Robusta estimation sample to 192 monthly observations compared to 288 for Arabica. The CFTC Disaggregated COT report was introduced in June 2006, so the Managed Money net position is missing for the first 77 months of the analysis period. Both gaps are handled by restricting estimation to complete-case sub-samples, but they imply that Robusta results and specifications including the COT variable are based on shorter and potentially less representative samples than the full 2000–2023 period.

5.2.6 Static Model Specifications

All six models assume a static relationship between coffee prices and their predictors, with coefficients or feature importances that are fixed over time or re-estimated on an expanding window that treats all historical observations equally. This assumption is at odds with the structural changes documented in the coffee market over the analysis period, including the progressive financialisation of commodity markets from the mid-2000s onward, the post-2008 shift in monetary policy regimes, and the supply chain disruptions of the COVID-19 period. Time-varying parameter models, such as rolling-window ML specifications with a fixed rather than expanding training window, would allow predictor relationships to evolve over time and may improve performance in structurally shifting environments.

5.2.7 ARIMAX Residual Autocorrelation

The ACF and PACF diagnostics of the ARIMAX residuals reveal an asymmetry between the two series. For Robusta, the ARIMA(3,0,1) error structure has fully absorbed the short-run autocorrelation, with no significant spike across all 24 lags. For Arabica, significant spikes remain at lags 1, 2, 5, 6, 16 and 24 in the ACF, and at lags 1, 5, 8 and 10 in the PACF, indicating that the ARIMA(1,0,0) error structure does not fully capture the medium-range autocorrelation dynamics of the Arabica residuals. A higher-order specification incorporating additional AR terms at lags 5 or 6 would likely reduce this residual dependence, though the walk-forward computational constraints imposed a maximum order of \(p=3\)in the auto.arima() search. This limitation does not invalidate the out-of-sample results given the \(R^2\) of 0.821 achieved for Arabica, but it represents a direction for future refinement.

6 Conclusion

This study estimated six forecasting models, two econometric benchmarks in the form of ARIMAX and Multiple Linear Regression and four machine learning algorithms comprising Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine and Artificial Neural Network, applied to monthly Arabica and Robusta coffee futures prices over the 2000–2023 period. Using a walk-forward expanding window validation protocol with an 80/20 train/test split, all models were evaluated on three out-of-sample metrics across a rich predictor set spanning macroeconomic, fundamental, climatic and speculative variables.

The principal empirical finding is that ARIMAX and XGBoost emerge as the strongest models for both coffee varieties under the baseline specification, achieving out-of-sample \(R^2\) values of 0.821 and 0.818 for Arabica and 0.929 and 0.796 for Robusta respectively. The strong performance of ARIMAX confirms that the persistence of prices around their own past values is a primary source of short-run predictability in coffee futures markets. The competitive performance of XGBoost demonstrates that gradient boosting can identify non-linear relationships among predictors that the linear regression component of ARIMAX cannot accommodate. The Multiple Linear Regression benchmark performs reasonably well for Arabica but collapses for Robusta at \(R^2\) = 0.276, confirming that a static linear model without temporal dynamics is insufficient when the estimation sample is short and predictors are highly correlated.

The variable importance analysis reveals that financial and speculative variables dominate the predictor rankings for both varieties. For Arabica, Sugar No.11 prices and the COT net Managed Money position are the two most influential predictors, reflecting the financialisation of the coffee futures market and the supply-side linkage between coffee and sugar in Brazil. For Robusta, WTI crude oil and CPI rank first, consistent with the energy-intensive production logistics of Vietnam and Indonesia and the price-elastic demand structure of the soluble coffee segment. Climate variables contribute relatively little predictive power at the one-month-ahead forecasting horizon, a finding explained by the long lag, typically six to twelve months, between climate shocks and their effect on prices through the production and inventory channel. This is not evidence that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices, but rather that a contemporaneous monthly model is not designed to capture this delayed transmission.

The three robustness checks yield several findings of independent interest. The disaggregated climate check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification: replacing the two global indices with the 28 individual national series systematically worsens performance across all ML models, validating the aggregation approach both statistically and economically. The variety-specific check reveals an important asymmetry: restricting climate and supply variables to Robusta-producing countries improves performance for four of the six models, with XGBoost reaching its strongest result at \(R^2\)= 0.849, while the same restriction uniformly deteriorates Arabica performance because the global indices are already dominated by Arabica-producing countries. The GDP growth check provides no support for including this variable as a predictor, with its marginal contribution found to be small, inconsistently signed across models and series, and confounded by the cost of moving to quarterly frequency that the absence of a monthly equivalent necessitates.

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these results. Estimating ML models on non-stationary price levels raises the risk of spurious correlations driven by common trends. The ANN exhibits instability under walk-forward re-estimation with small training samples. The hyperparameter tuning procedure relies on a single pre-loop validation split rather than a fully nested walk-forward search. The national climate averages do not account for the distribution of coffee cultivation within each country. And all six models assume static predictor relationships over a 24-year period that witnessed substantial structural change in the coffee market.

These limitations point to several directions for future work. Cointegration-based error correction specifications would better handle the non-stationarity of the series while preserving the long-run equilibrium relationships among prices and fundamentals. Incorporating lagged climate variables at three, six and twelve months would allow the model to capture the delayed weather-to-price transmission channel that contemporaneous specifications cannot exploit. Recurrent neural network architectures, in particular Long Short-Term Memory networks, would address the ANN instability by maintaining a hidden state across time steps rather than reinitialising at each walk-forward step. Finally, rolling-window or regime-switching specifications would allow predictor relationships to evolve over time, better reflecting the structural shifts the coffee market has undergone over the analysis period.

From a practical standpoint, the results suggest that market participants seeking short-run price signals for coffee would benefit most from monitoring speculative positioning in the futures market and energy prices rather than focusing on supply fundamentals or climate conditions at monthly frequency. The variety-specific results further suggest that Robusta-focused analysts should track supply conditions in Vietnam and Indonesia specifically, as global aggregates dilute the variety-relevant signal. The consistent performance of multiple model families across both series and multiple specifications strengthens the reliability of these conclusions and suggests that the predictor set constructed in this study captures genuine and robust information about the drivers of coffee futures prices.

Claude (Anthropic) was used as an artificial intelligence assistant in the preparation of this thesis, including support for writing and structuring the text and for the design and debugging of the R data processing and modelling pipeline implemented in Quarto.

## Overview of the Dataset

This study draws on eight distinct data sources covering the period from January 2000 to December 2023, yielding 288 monthly observations for the main analysis. The choice of this starting point rests on three considerations. First, the International Coffee Organization suspended its export quota system in 1989, and its definitive abandonment over the following years produced a decade of institutional transition that reshaped the price formation environment prevailing over the analysis period (Lewin et al., 2004). Coffee price data from before 2000 therefore reflect a structurally different market environment, and including them would introduce regime-change breaks that complicate time series modelling. Second, the ERA5 reanalysis dataset used for the climate variables reaches its highest spatial and temporal reliability from 2000 onward, corresponding to the transition to the modern satellite era (Hersbach et al., 2020). Third, two variables used throughout the analysis remain only partially available within this window: the CFTC Disaggregated COT report starts in June 2006, and Robusta futures prices from Refinitiv start in January 2008. The analysis ends in December 2023, the last month for which all data sources were simultaneously available at the time of data collection.

*This chunk produces the variable summary table presented in the text. Each row corresponds to one variable retained in the final dataset, grouped by category.
